implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the shareable completion handle but not the registry: std::future is move-only, while std::shared_future is copyable and its get() may be called by many threads, so the idiom is a mutex-guarded map from key to std::shared_future<T> (or to an entry owning the promise and a waiter count). The leader creates the promise and publishes the shared_future into the map before starting work, sets value or exception on the promise, and erases the key with the lock held; waiters copy the shared_future out of the map and call get() outside the lock, so the mutex is never held across the computation or across a blocking wait. Erasing at completion keeps the map an in-flight registry; keeping the entry would silently turn it into a cache.
pitfalls: std::future is move-only: store and hand out std::shared_future (the result of share()), or waiters cannot copy the handle out of the registry.
get() re-throws the exception stored by set_exception for every waiter - the intended shared error, but it means the leader's error is fanned out and each waiter must handle it.
Hold the registry mutex only for map access: waiting on a shared_future or running the loader with the lock held serializes every unrelated key.
Erase on completion, not on announcement: a waiter that copies the handle stays valid, but a late joiner after the erase correctly starts a second flight.
Outstanding shared_futures keep the shared state and the result alive, so a registry that never erases entries becomes an unbounded cache.

variants.name: Folly SharedPromise/Future (C++17)
variants.implementation_notes: Folly ships both halves as first-class types: folly::SharedPromise<T> is a promise whose getFuture() may be called many times, so one in-flight computation hands out any number of futures, and a ConcurrentHashMap or mutex-guarded map keyed by the coalescing key is a thin registry on top. Future/SemiFuture continuation and timeout facilities let each waiter wait with its own deadline without touching the shared execution. Choose this form where folly is already a dependency; the standard-library form needs no third-party code.
pitfalls: SharedPromise::getFuture may be called many times, but setValue/setException only wins once; a second completion attempt is ignored or throws, so the flight must publish exactly once.
Work submitted with runAsync runs on the folly executor: keep the registry erase on an ensure/continuation rather than on a waiter's thread, or the entry leaks when no waiter is left.
A folly::Future chain keeps its shared state alive; a registry that never erases completed entries becomes an unbounded cache.
